summary:
ClimateLens is a browser-based teaching platform that turns NASA Earth data into a guided inquiry a student can finish in a single lesson. A learner starts on a ring of five Southeast Asian islands, chooses Singapore, and lands on a data-rich island with twelve real locations. Each location opens a small portrait, and every question — is this city getting hotter, wetter, windier? — is answered by the server alone: it retrieves NASA POWER data for 2001–2025 and fits an ordinary least squares trend with Newey–West standard errors, reporting a 95% confidence interval and a p value, expressed per decade.

The interface follows the scientific method instead of hiding it. Students predict first, then observe, then compare their city against another, then write their own conclusion and export a report as PDF. An optional AI tutor helps phrase a question but never computes statistics, and disappears quietly if it is unavailable. MODIS land-surface-temperature imagery gives each neighbourhood a face.

It matters because climate literacy usually arrives as finished graphs. ClimateLens hands students the evidence and the uncertainty, so they learn to read a trend line — and its confidence interval — as a claim they can check. The site, data and code are public.
details:
ClimateLens is a web application developed for the Earth System Trend Detective challenge in the 2026 NASA International Space Apps Challenge. It combines time-series visualization and statistical analysis in a guided investigation of five climate variables across five Southeast Asian cities: Singapore, Kuala Lumpur, Jakarta, Bangkok, and Ho Chi Minh City.

Challenge alignment
The challenge asks teams to identify environmental change in NASA data. ClimateLens does this with NASA POWER data for 2001-2025 and concentrates on the step that follows detection: deciding whether a pattern is a sustained trend, how uncertain it is, and what it can and cannot support. Students do this work themselves, so the platform builds the reasoning skills that interpreting Earth system data requires.

Investigation approach
Every investigation follows the same six steps. Changing the city, variable, years, or question clears earlier results, so the evidence on screen always matches the current settings. A written conclusion is preserved but must be reviewed again by the student.

1. Ask. The student chooses a city, variable, and years, or types a question. ClimateLens interprets a typed question with keyword rules and proposes settings. The student confirms them; an ambiguous question never runs an analysis silently.
2. Predict. The student may record a prediction before seeing the data. ClimateLens asks for the prediction before the data are shown; the step can be skipped.
3. Observe. The student reads the annual chart and table. ClimateLens fetches monthly NASA POWER data and plots annual values. The fitted line and statistical explanation stay hidden until the student expands the statistics section.
4. Interpret. The student reviews the rate of change per decade, its 95% confidence interval, the p-value, and the limitations, then acknowledges them. ClimateLens calculates the statistics on the server and explains units, uncertainty, and limits.
5. Conclude. The student writes a conclusion in their own words. ClimateLens never edits the conclusion, and the workflow cannot show as complete until the student has written one.
6. Export. The student downloads a PDF report; annual data are also available as CSV. ClimateLens builds the report from results held on the server, and a report exported without valid evidence is clearly marked incomplete.

A city comparison uses matching years to display two trend estimates side by side. It is descriptive: testing whether the slopes differ would require a separate analysis.

Data and variables
Air temperature (T2M, degrees Celsius): annual value is the mean of monthly values, weighted by days in each month.
Precipitation (PRECTOTCORR, mm/day): daily rate multiplied by days in each month, summed to mm/year.
Relative humidity (RH2M, percent): mean of monthly values, weighted by days in each month.
Wind speed (WS10M, m/s): mean of monthly values, weighted by days in each month.
Solar radiation (ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN, kW-hr/m2/day): day-weighted mean of daily energy, not an annual total.

Data come from the NASA POWER monthly point service for the grid location nearest each city. POWER's meteorological values derive from NASA's MERRA-2 assimilation model (about 0.5 by 0.625 degree grid) and its solar values from satellite-based CERES products (1 degree grid), so each series is an estimate for the area around a city rather than a station measurement. The pipeline checks every returned unit against the expected one, ignores POWER's 13th-month annual summary, and excludes any year with a missing or invalid month without interpolation. Availability of all five variables for all five cities has been checked against live NASA POWER responses. Source: NASA POWER documentation, https://power.larc.nasa.gov/docs/services/api/temporal/monthly/

Statistical method
An ordinary least squares line estimates the linear trend. Standard errors use the Newey-West (Bartlett kernel) covariance from statsmodels, with a finite-sample correction and a lag of floor(4(n/100)^(2/9)), at least one, to allow for correlation between consecutive years. Confidence intervals and p-values use approximate t inference, and slopes and intervals are reported per decade. Inference requires at least ten consecutive complete years and is withheld for constant series. The slope, standard error, p-value, and confidence interval have been checked against independent calculations. A nonsignificant result does not mean that no change occurred.

Tools and technologies
The frontend uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with SVG for interactive charts and no separate build step. A Python backend built with FastAPI and served by Uvicorn provides the web pages and API. HTTPX retrieves NASA POWER records. NumPy, SciPy, and statsmodels support statistical analysis. ReportLab generates PDF reports with a chart that labels axes and units, annual values, source information, limitations, and the student's conclusion. Chinese text is rendered with an embedded Noto Sans SC subset so it displays in readers without a Chinese font. Annual data can also be downloaded as CSV.

Development and testing
Development began with the data pipeline, followed by the analysis module, the student workflow, and finally export. Python and JavaScript tests cover data processing, statistical calculations, and interface behavior. Offline tests use clearly labeled synthetic fixtures that are never presented as NASA data, and a separate live NASA check runs against the real service. GitHub Actions runs the offline tests and the live check on each pull request, and a browser walkthrough script that exercises the full student journey is included in the repository.

Limitations and safeguards
- Each series describes a grid cell near the city and is derived from model and satellite products, not station records.
- The record holds at most 25 annual values, so inference is approximate.
- A linear trend describes 2001-2025. It cannot establish a cause or predict the future.
- Repeatedly choosing variables and years can raise the chance of false positives, and no multiple-testing correction is applied.
- Incomplete years are excluded, never interpolated.
